To be remembered after death is what every human wants.

Humans seem to want to be remembered. This can be understood. What is a bit harder to understand is what a person wants to be remembered for.

As in: 'I don't want to be remembered for the things I haven't done' (W. Somerset Maugham). Or: 'To be remembered, that's all we can really ask for' (The Boat that Rocked). Or even: 'Even when he is forgotten long after he is dead, the echoes of his being shall live on into eternity' (The Boat that Rocked, again).

Incidentally the quotation from the film The Boat that Rocked (my favourite film) is taken from the real-life radio disc jockey Quentin Crisp, who had a great sense of humour about life and death. He is also remembered for the line, 'I'm dying to die,' and he said he wanted his ashes placed near the Royal Albert Hall 'so that when, in heaven, I ask St Peter where we are, he can answer: "Just over the Royal Albert Hall." '

Unfortunately, most people are remembered only too well (for the wrong reasons of course). I have in mind people like Hitler, Stalin, Pol Pot and Mao Zedong; their deeds have blighted the lives of millions. But they are not alone in not being remembered for the right reasons.

Some politicians try to make a name for themselves by making grand promises, saying how they'd lead the country forward. You know the sort of thing: 'Education! Education! Education!' For some reason, their speeches are always greeted with rapturous applause and people keep on voting them back in. But once they assume office, they come across like William Shakespeare's character Macbeth: 'Full of sound and fury, signifying nothing!'

And then there are politicians who go underground once they lose their posts only to resurface later when the heat is off. Some remain quiet only to become active once again in their political parties. And there are those leaders who return to seek the limelight after their failed bids for office when the next general election is in sight.<eos>
